quote: A useful prompt makes the important details impossible to miss.
example: “Create a one-page project update for senior leaders. Include the current status, the main risk, and the decision needed by Friday.”

quote: Clarity begins when you name the question you actually need answered.
example: Instead of “Tell me about our website,” ask “Which pages have the highest exit rates, and what should we investigate first?”

quote: More words don’t guarantee more information; relevant details do.
example: “Suggest three low-cost ways to reduce meeting overruns for a 12-person remote team” is more useful than a long description of the company that doesn’t affect the suggestions.

quote: A precise question turns a broad topic into a workable task.
example: “Explain customer retention” becomes “List three reasons first-time subscribers may cancel within 30 days, and suggest one way to test each reason.”

quote: Good thinking separates what is known from what is assumed.
example: “Known: orders fell 8% this month. Assumption: the new checkout page contributed. Suggest data we should check before drawing a conclusion.”

quote: The right context can make a short instruction more powerful than a long one.
example: “Rewrite this error message for first-time users who may not know what a ‘sync’ is.”

quote: Specificity is not extra detail; it is detail that changes the answer.
example: “Recommend a laptop” becomes “Recommend a laptop under $1,000 for frequent travel, long battery life, and everyday spreadsheet work.”

quote: When a request is vague, the result has to guess.
example: Instead of “Make this better,” ask “Make this announcement easier to scan while keeping the date, location, and registration instructions unchanged.”

quote: Make the goal clear before you ask for the route.
example: “I need to prepare a 10-minute briefing for a budget review. Suggest an outline that highlights costs, risks, and decisions.”

quote: A strong prompt tells the reader what success should look like.
example: “Draft a reply to this customer complaint. It succeeds if the customer knows what we will do, by when, and whom to contact.”

quote: Useful information narrows the possibilities that matter.
example: “Suggest team-building activities” becomes “Suggest three 30-minute activities for a hybrid team of eight that require no special equipment.”

quote: If a sentence could fit any situation, it may explain none of them.
example: Instead of “How can we plan better?”, ask “Our design review happens before requirements are approved, so work gets repeated. How should we reorder these two steps?”

quote: Good questions reveal the choices hidden inside a problem.
example: “Should we launch next month?” becomes “What do we gain and risk by launching next month rather than waiting until the support team is fully trained?”

quote: The best constraints don’t block ideas; they point them in the right direction.
example: “Suggest ways to welcome new customers using our existing email platform, with no added software and no more than two staff hours per week.”

quote: Precision is the art of keeping what matters and removing what doesn’t.
example: “Summarize this report in 150 words for department leads. Focus on findings that affect next quarter’s staffing plan.”

quote: A better answer often starts with a better-defined task.
example: “Help with my presentation” becomes “Create a five-slide outline explaining the project delay, its impact, and the recovery plan.”

quote: State the audience, purpose, and limits—and let the details do their work.
example: “Write a plain-language guide for first-time volunteers explaining check-in. Keep it under 300 words and include where to go and whom to ask for help.”

quote: Clear instructions reduce guesswork for everyone involved.
example: “Review this draft for spelling and unclear sentences only. Keep the author’s tone and do not add new claims.”

quote: Information becomes useful when it helps someone decide what to do next.
example: “Our delivery delays rose last month. Identify the three most useful data points to review before deciding whether to change the shipping process.”

quote: Think carefully about what the answer needs to know before asking it to respond.
example: “Create a five-day dinner plan for two: 30 minutes of preparation at most, under $60 in total, and no nuts.”

quote: Define the decision before gathering the details.
example: “We need to choose a launch date. Compare these two dates by engineering readiness, customer impact, and support coverage.”

quote: A useful question makes its boundaries visible.
example: “Explain renewable energy” becomes “Compare solar and wind power for a small business seeking to reduce daytime electricity costs.”

quote: Facts, assumptions, and preferences are different kinds of information.
example: “Fact: the team has four weeks. Assumption: the vendor can deliver the data export. Preference: avoid adding weekend work.”

quote: The audience changes what counts as a clear answer.
example: “Explain the outage to customers in plain language, focusing on what happened, what services were affected, and what happens next.”

quote: A prompt improves when it names the shape of a useful result.
example: “Return a comparison of the three proposals with columns for cost, timeline, key risk, and open question.”

quote: Specific examples turn abstract expectations into visible targets.
example: “Write the reminder email in a direct, practical tone, like this line: ‘Send the draft by Thursday so the team can review it Friday.’”

quote: A good prompt distinguishes the main task from the supporting material.
example: “Summarize the attached interview notes in five themes. Use the project brief only to clarify terminology.”

quote: Useful analysis starts by naming the criteria.
example: “Assess these vendors on implementation time, accessibility, annual cost, and data portability.”

quote: When priorities compete, say which one leads.
example: “Keep the explanation under 200 words; prioritize accuracy over covering every background detail.”

quote: A well-framed problem points toward a relevant solution.
example: “Meeting notes are often missing action owners. Suggest a lightweight process that captures an owner and due date for each task.”

quote: Ask for uncertainty to be shown, not hidden.
example: “Separate confirmed information from estimates, and flag any conclusion that depends on an unverified assumption.”

quote: The most helpful summary preserves decisions, not just discussion.
example: “Summarize the meeting under three labels: decisions made, actions with owners, and unresolved questions.”

quote: A question becomes actionable when it connects insight to a next step.
example: “What is the most common reason customers abandon checkout, and what small test could help us investigate it?”

quote: Name what must stay unchanged when asking for a revision.
example: “Shorten this contract summary to 100 words. Don’t change any dates, amounts or names of the parties.”

quote: A prompt should distinguish what to produce from what to avoid.
example: “Write a neutral product description for first-time buyers. Avoid unsupported performance claims and unexplained technical terms.”

quote: Useful questions make room for more than one plausible answer.
example: “Give two possible explanations for the increase in support requests, along with evidence that would help distinguish them.”

quote: Clear thinking turns a pile of details into a structure people can use.
example: “Organize these research notes by customer need, supporting observation, and possible product implication.”

quote: An answer can only be as specific as the situation you describe.
example: “Suggest a weekly schedule for a two-person bakery that opens at 7 a.m., closes on Mondays, and bakes bread the night before.”

quote: If anyone could have sent your prompt, the answer will be written for anyone.
example: Instead of “Write a cover letter,” ask “Write a cover letter for a junior data analyst role, drawing on my three years in retail operations and my SQL course.”

quote: Share the details the task needs, not the ones it doesn’t.
example: “Summarize these case notes for a policy review. I’ve replaced names and employee IDs with [NAME] and [ID].”

quote: Give the model a role when the role changes what it should notice.
example: “Act as a first-time user reviewing this sign-up page. List every point where you would hesitate or be unsure what to do next.”

quote: The first answer is a draft; the follow-up is where you steer.
example: “Good start. Drop the third option, which needs budget we don’t have, and expand the second into steps for next week.”

quote: Big tasks get better answers one step at a time.
example: “First, list the questions this proposal must answer for the board. Don’t draft anything yet.”

quote: When a problem keeps coming back, ask about the system, not the event.
example: “Our support backlog keeps growing even after we hired two people. Map the handoffs and incentives that could be feeding it.”

quote: Ask why more than once before you accept a cause.
example: “Our release slipped because testing ran late. Ask ‘why’ four more times and show the chain of causes.”

quote: Ask for the case against your plan before you commit to it.
example: “Here is our plan to move every team to weekly releases. Give the strongest argument against it.”

quote: Imagine the failure first; it shows you what to protect.
example: “Imagine this product launch has failed six months from now. List the three most likely reasons.”

quote: A confident tone is not the same as a certain answer.
example: “For each recommendation, say how confident you are and what evidence would change your view.”

quote: Start from the person’s friction, not from the feature.
example: “Describe our check-in process from the point of view of a parent arriving late with two children. Where does it break down?”

quote: When you are stuck between two options, ask for a third.
example: “We need faster approvals and tighter spending control. Don’t choose between them; propose a process that serves both.”

quote: Every yes spends something you could have used elsewhere.
example: “We can build only one of these three features this quarter. For each, say what we give up by choosing it.”

quote: Remove the noise before you ask for the signal.
example: “From these survey comments, set aside general praise and one-off requests. Group the complaints that appear more than once.”

quote: Data becomes information when it answers a question someone has.
example: “Here are last quarter’s sales by region. Which figures matter for deciding where to hire our next sales rep?”

quote: Point the model to its sources, and ask it to stay inside them.
example: “Answer using only the attached policy document. If it doesn’t cover the question, say so.”

quote: Choose the format by how the answer will be used.
example: “Give me a checklist I can print and tick off during the office move, grouped by room.”

quote: The same facts need different words for different readers.
example: “Explain the new expense policy twice: once for managers who approve claims, and once for staff who submit them.”

quote: Context you set once can shape every answer after it.
example: “For this conversation: I manage six nurses in a small clinic. Keep all advice practical and within our current staffing.”

quote: Let the model ask before it guesses.
example: “Before you draft the plan, ask me up to five questions about anything you would otherwise have to assume.”

quote: Check the answer against the question you asked, not against how good it sounds.
example: “Review your previous answer against my original request. List anything I asked for that it missed.”

quote: An average can hide the story; ask for the breakdown.
example: “Average delivery time looks steady. Split it by region and carrier, and show where it rose.”
